analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to cover HIV prevention drugs at no cost to patients and bans discrimination against PrEP users.
analysis.headline: The PrEP Access and Coverage Act drew 190 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a committee markup or a House floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require nearly every type of health coverage — private plans, employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service — to cover drugs that prevent HIV, plus the lab tests and doctor visits needed to take them, with no copays, deductibles, or prior-approval hurdles. It would also make it illegal for life, disability, and long-term care insurers to deny coverage or raise premiums because someone takes HIV prevention medication. And it would fund free PrEP and PEP access for uninsured people through grants and a public education campaign.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of HIV. Today many can't afford the drugs or the regular lab tests PrEP requires, and insurers can deny them life or disability coverage for taking it. The bill removes the cost barrier in both public and private plans, guarantees access for the uninsured through federal grants, and bars the insurance discrimination.

how_it_helps.text: Requires private plans, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, FEHB, VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service to cover FDA-approved HIV prevention drugs, lab work, and follow-up care with no cost-sharing, effective for plan years starting January 2023 [S3].
Bans preauthorization requirements for HIV prevention drugs — insurers can only require prior approval for a drug if they cover a therapeutically equivalent alternative without any [S3].

Makes it unlawful for life, disability, and long-term care insurers to deny, limit, or reprice coverage because someone takes HIV prevention medication, enforceable by state insurance regulators [S3].

Creates grants for states, tribes, and clinics like federally qualified health centers to provide PrEP and PEP to uninsured and underinsured people, and directs the CDC to run public and provider education campaigns aimed at the communities where use is lowest [S3].
Requires HHS to update privacy rules so someone on a family plan can use these benefits without the policyholder being told [S3].
Includes a private right of action, letting individuals sue for violations and recover attorney fees if they win [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, who would absorb the cost of covering drugs and related services without charging patients, spreading it across premiums; life, disability, and long-term care insurers, who would lose an underwriting tool; and federal and state programs, which would fund the grants and absorb new coverage obligations in Medicare, Medicaid, and VA.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating all cost-sharing in private plans and public programs raises premiums and program spending; the bill sets no spending cap, only authorizing 'such sums as may be necessary' for the grants through 2028 [S3].

The insurance non-discrimination rule bars pricing or denial based on PrEP use 'without any additional actuarial risks,' a limit on how life, disability, and long-term care insurers underwrite, which those insurers would argue forces other policyholders to absorb the difference [S3].

The preauthorization ban is not absolute: a plan can still require prior approval for a particular drug if it covers a therapeutically equivalent one without any, so choice of specific drugs can still be steered [S3].

Enforcement of the insurance non-discrimination rule depends on state regulators acting 'as are specifically authorized under the laws of such State,' so protection varies by state and some states may have no enforcement path [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete: PrEP cuts the risk of getting HIV from sex by about 99 percent, yet in 2019 only about 23 percent of the roughly 1.1 million people who could benefit filled prescriptions, with use heavily skewed by race and income [S3]. The costs — higher premiums and federal spending — are real but are the standard trade-off of a preventive-coverage mandate. The main design weakness is the open-ended funding authorization and state-dependent enforcement of the insurance rule.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to seven House committees, then sent down to two subcommittees, and never got a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on December 1, 2021 [S1].

The Speaker referred it to seven committees — Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Reform, Ways and Means, Veterans' Affairs, Armed Services, Natural Resources, and Financial Services — splitting jurisdiction so no single committee had to move it [S5].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on December 2, 2021, and again on January 6, 2022, and to the Natural Resources Indigenous Peoples Subcommittee on December 14, 2021; no further action followed [S5].
It attracted 190 cosponsors, every one a House Democrat, and none of the seven committees ever held a markup or reported the bill [S4] [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill never having reached the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, who avoided a mandate to cover HIV prevention drugs and services without charging patients, and life, disability, and long-term care insurers, who kept the ability to consider PrEP use when pricing or denying coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers that avoided the coverage mandate

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 1, 2021 and led 33 original cosponsors [S1] [S3].

for.name: 190 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 190 were Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote in the two years it was pending; the action history shows no floor consideration [S5].

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee; it sat in the Health Subcommittee with no markup after referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 190 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill died without any roll-call vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill would force private plans to cover HIV prevention drugs, lab work, and follow-up care with no cost-sharing and no preauthorization. Insurers avoided this mandate when the bill died, and the cost of that avoidance is borne by people who can't afford PrEP.

industries.industry: Life, disability, and long-term care insurers
industries.note: The bill would make it unlawful to deny, limit, or reprice these policies because someone takes HIV prevention medication. Keeping the status quo lets insurers continue using PrEP use in underwriting, a barrier for people trying to protect their health.
Universal no-cost-sharing coverage across public and private programs would expand the market for FDA-approved HIV prevention drugs, including brand-name products alongside generics.

industries.industry: Community health centers and public health programs
industries.note: The bill authorizes grants through 2028 for states, tribes, and clinics such as federally qualified health centers to deliver PrEP and PEP to uninsured people.
